Set an experimental incomplete block design

Source: R/randomize.R
randomize.Rd

Generate a sequentially balanced incomplete block design for tricot trials. Every prefix of the design is kept close to balanced, so the design stays good when only the first packages are distributed or returned.

randomize(
  npackages,
  itemnames,
  ncomp = 3,
  availability = NULL,
  props = NULL,
  ridge = 0.001,
  polish = FALSE,
  schedule = TRUE,
  ...
)

randomise(...)

Arguments

npackages

an integer for the number of incomplete blocks (packages)

itemnames

a character vector with the unique names of the items

ncomp

an integer for the number of items in each block (default 3)

availability

optional, an integer vector with the maximum number of plots for each item in itemnames

props

optional, a numeric vector with the desired proportions for each item in itemnames

ridge

small ridge added to the Laplacian to handle a disconnected early design. Disconnected components are then strongly penalised

polish

logical, if TRUE run a final local search on the position balance of the complete design. This can reduce the position balance of prefixes

schedule

logical, if TRUE (the default) use the replication schedule as primary key. If FALSE, select on A-optimality alone (slower, similar quality)

...

arguments of the previous algorithm, such as comp, are accepted for compatibility and ignored with a warning

Value

A data.frame with one row per package and the columns item_A, item_B, ...

Details

At each step the function

  1. keeps only blocks whose items all have remaining quota (hard availability);

  2. prefers blocks with the most items behind their replication schedule;

  3. breaks ties by the exact A-optimality gain of the prefix, evaluated for all tied candidates with a rank-k update of the Laplacian inverse;

  4. breaks remaining ties at random.

Item order within blocks is then balanced sequentially across positions. Call set.seed() before the function to make the design reproducible.

References

Bailey and Cameron (2004). Combinations of optimal designs. https://webspace.maths.qmul.ac.uk/l.h.soicher/designtheory.org/library/preprints/optimal.pdf

Author

Jacob van Etten

Examples

set.seed(1)
design = randomize(npackages = 20,
                   itemnames = c("apple", "banana", "grape", "mango", "orange"))
table(unlist(design))

# limited availability of some items
set.seed(1)
randomize(npackages = 20,
          itemnames = c("apple", "banana", "grape", "mango", "orange"),
          availability = c(5, 8, 50, 50, 50))
